model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Havannah on a 15x15 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opp: list[tuple[int, int]], valid_mask) -> tuple[int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples for player-0 stones. - `opp` is a list of (row, col) tuples for player-1 stones. - `valid_mask` is a 2D array (shape NxN) where True marks playable cells on the Havannah board. - Rows and columns are 0-indexed in `0..14`, matching `valid_mask` indices. - A player wins when they complete one of three different structures from unbroken lines, or paths, of connected stones, all of their colour:- A ring is a loop around one or more cells (no matter whether the encircled cells are occupied by any player or empty[3]) - - A bridge, which connects any two of the six corner cells of the board - - A fork, which connects any three edges of the board; corner points are not considered parts of an edge - Note that the board is represented as a 2D array however internally it is a hexagonal grid. This requires extra spatial reasoning to determine the winning structures.Every stone not on the edge of the board is touching exactly 6 other stones (since they are hexagonal). - Two of those 6 stones are in the same column, two are in the left column, and two are in the right column. - Example: The store located at (4, 1) [i.e. b5] is touching b6 (5, 1) and b4 (3, 1) - and to its left is touching a4 (3, 0) and a5 (4, 0) - and to its right is touching c5 (4, 2) and c4 (3, 2) # Action / Return Format - Return a single move as a tuple `(row, col)`. - The chosen coordinate must satisfy `valid_mask[row][col] == True` and be unoccupied. - There is no pass move; always place a stone. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm working through the hex board geometry for a Havannah board with side length 8, figuring out how the 169 valid cells map onto the 15x15 rhombus array using axial coordinate bounds.

Looking at the sample neighbor relations given, though, they don't match standard axial adjacency — the left/right neighbor offsets suggest instead an offset (odd-q/even-q style) coordinate layout where adjacency depends on column parity, so I need to reconsider how this board actually encodes neighbors before assuming pure axial coordinates.

Given the ambiguity, I think the safer strategy is to infer the neighbor structure directly from the valid_mask itself at runtime, checking whether it forms a rhombus shape or an offset hexagon, then picking the matching adjacency rule. Testing this against the specific example cell should clarify which coordinate convention is actually in play.

I'm trying to visualize the actual hexagon shape of the board under even-q offset coordinates — figuring out how columns of varying length (15 cells in the middle tapering to 8 at the edges) would need to be vertically positioned so the whole thing forms a proper hexagon with six corners.

Given how uncertain this geometric reasoning is, I decide it's better to write code that detects the coordinate layout directly from the valid_mask at runtime rather than hardcode assumptions — checking whether valid cells match a diagonal band pattern like |r-c|≤7, which would indicate axial coordinates, and then verifying which neighbor offsets are consistent with that layout.

For adjacent columns c and c-1, I need to figure out the vertical offset relationship by comparing their top row positions — if they match, column c-1 is shifted down half a row and neighbors would be (r-1,c-1) and (r,c-1); if offset by one, the relationship flips accordingly.

I realize it's cleaner to just directly compute each cell's vertical position as row + half-integer shift depending on column parity, then find neighbors by matching positions offset by ±0.5 rather than reasoning through cases separately for each half of the hexagon.

Rather than solving this fully generally, I'm sketching a detection scheme instead: checking whether the grid is a rhombus, a column-hexagon, or a row-hexagon shape, then falling back to the parity rule if none match. For the column-hexagon case, I'm working out neighbor relationships by computing a shift value per column and comparing adjacent shifts to decide which rows connect, verifying it against the example column shifts.

Now I need to identify corners (3 valid neighbors) and edges (4 valid neighbors) generically, then group boundary cells into six connected edge components regardless of layout, though I still need to check whether adjacent boundary cells actually connect across each edge.

For win detection, I'm planning to implement group tracking via union-find or BFS, recording which edges and corners each group touches, plus logic to detect when a placed stone completes a ring enclosing at least one cell.

For ring detection, the key idea is checking whether the complement of the group has a component that doesn't reach the board boundary—meaning it's fully enclosed. I need to consider edge cases like a solid hexagonal blob of stones, where the interior cell is part of the same group rather than a separate enclosed region, and whether that still counts as forming a ring per the rules.

I'm working out a general definition: a ring exists if some cell x has all its escape paths to the border blocked by the group, checking this both for cells inside and cells that are part of the group itself by testing removal. Since I only need to check rings involving the newly placed stone, I'll implement a flood-fill test to see whether the placed stone (or a cell adjacent to it) becomes enclosed once the group forms.

To make this efficient, I'm considering flood-filling the complement of the stone set once to find which regions touch the border, then checking each stone by seeing whether its non-group neighbors all fall into enclosed regions -- though I need to be careful about cases where an adjacent stone is also part of the same group.

I'm also weighing whether a stone completely surrounded by six own-color stones counts as a ring in the arena's actual implementation, and deciding to count it since official rules do, even though I'm unsure if the arena matches. I'm double-checking that enclosed complement regions truly correspond to connected rings of stones, since a ring requires the boundary cells to form a connected loop within the same group.

Given the tight time budget, my strategy is: play a winning move if I have one, block the opponent's winning move if they have one (prioritizing overlap with my own plans if there are multiple), otherwise fall back to heuristics with shallow lookahead for double threats, and evaluate positions using something like a shortest-path/resistance measure between corners for group connectivity.

I'm designing this via Dijkstra-style distances—treating my own stones as free passage, empty cells as cost 1, and opponent stones as blocked—to compute connection costs between corners and forks between edge triples. I'll handle ring formation separately through direct tactical threat detection rather than distance metrics, since rings don't fit the same connectivity model.

But I'm realizing the computational cost is a real problem: running full Dijkstra or 0-1 BFS from 12 sources across 169 candidate moves for both players is going to be far too slow for real-time play, likely several seconds per decision. I need to cut this down by prefiltering candidates to a smaller set near existing stones or using a faster heuristic before doing the expensive distance computation.

My plan is to narrow the field to about 30 promising candidate moves (adjacent to existing stones or on current shortest paths), run the full evaluation only on those, and add a time budget so I can gracefully fall back to the best move found if I run out of time. For move selection priority, I'm laying out the tactical checklist: check for an immediate win, then check for blocking the opponent's immediate win (picking the best blocking option if multiple threats exist), then look for moves that create a double threat for myself.

A double threat is essentially unstoppable if it produces two distinct winning cells, since the opponent can only occupy one cell per turn and placing a stone elsewhere doesn't disrupt my existing connections. To detect this I'd need to test, for each candidate move, how many winning cells remain afterward, but doing a full win-test for every empty cell for every candidate move is way too expensive computationally.

A smarter approach uses precomputed union-find groups with edge/corner bitmasks: a cell becomes a winning move if it merges groups whose combined edges/corners satisfy the bridge or fork condition, or if it completes a ring. For ring detection specifically, I'm considering the six neighbors of a candidate cell in cyclic order and checking whether two same-group neighbors close a cycle around it.

Doing a full BFS after each move to detect enclosed regions would be too slow across many candidate moves, so I need a cheaper necessary condition to prune when a ring check is even worth running. I'm thinking the key signal is whether w's neighbors within the same group form a contiguous arc versus a split arrangement — if they're split (non-adjacent to each other around w), that's a strong candidate for ring formation, letting me skip the expensive check otherwise.

Testing this against a ring-of-6 example: if w's G-neighbors are non-contiguous (separated by an empty cell), enclosure works cleanly, but if the ring's center is also a stone, the neighbors become contiguous and my condition fails to flag it as enclosing. So I need to broaden the rule to also catch cases where w is adjacent to a stone that's already surrounded.

I need to be careful about border cells where the neighbor cycle is incomplete—treating invalid positions as non-S, then checking whether the S-neighbors split into two separate arcs versus one contiguous arc determines whether a ring could form.

If placing w truly encloses a region R, then w sits on the boundary between R and the outside, meaning it has neighbors in both R and outside. Since consecutive neighbors of w are mutually adjacent in a hex grid, these two groups must be separated by S-neighbors on both sides—unless the separation happens through off-board positions, but R can't touch the board edge so that shouldn't be possible.

For corners with three consecutive off-board positions, the flanking cells are still edge cells, so this confirms condition (a) is necessary for enclosure once the S-separators exist along both sides. This means I can check ring formation quickly with the simple filter before falling back to full BFS verification only when needed, keeping the winning-cell computation fast across all empty cells.

Now I'm sketching the policy logic: first check if I have a winning cell and return it immediately, otherwise check if the opponent has winning cells and must be blocked, evaluating candidate blocks by their overall position score if there are multiple threats to choose from.

For each candidate move, I simulate placing my stone and check whether it creates two or more winning cells afterward — a double threat that forces a win, since opponent's own winning cells stay unaffected by my move. I also want to watch for opponent moves that would create a double threat for them, collecting those into a set so I can prioritize playing there defensively when such threats exist, falling back to broader candidates when none do.

A new winning cell after placing o must be adjacent to the merged group containing o, which narrows candidates but is still costly for large groups. I'm considering building a Board class with a winning_cells function that reconstructs union-find from scratch each time — roughly 1-2ms per call, but running it across all candidate moves for both players could total around half a second, so I need to look for ways to optimize by reusing the union-find structure instead of rebuilding it every time.

I can precompute liberties for each group, then for a candidate move m, merge the liberties of the adjacent groups plus its own empty neighbors to get the merged group's liberties directly — this avoids rebuilding the whole union-find and only checks cells that touch the merged group, since any newly winning cell must connect through it.

For speed, I'm thinking of maintaining a mutable board with an incremental union-find that recomputes per candidate placement rather than from scratch — roughly 0.3ms per recompute, so testing all ~169 candidates for both players stays around 170ms. After placing a stone I only need to check empty cells that share a root with the merged group before undoing the move, which keeps this tractable while I move on to designing the evaluation function using distance BFS for the top candidates.

For evaluating a position, I'm defining cost per cell (0 for own stones, 1 for empty, infinite for opponent stones) and running 0-1 BFS from each corner and edge to get distance fields. I'm using these distances to estimate bridge costs between corner pairs and fork costs between triples of edges as approximate Steiner-tree junction costs, converting distances into threat scores via an exponential decay, then combining my threat score against the opponent's to get the position's evaluation, while leaving ring detection as a rough heuristic for now since it's harder to approximate this way.

Placing my stone naturally increases opponent costs where it blocks their paths, so tactical detection at shallow depth should catch ring threats without extra machinery. For move ordering, I'll restrict candidates to empty cells near existing stones plus centrally scored ones, ranking each by how much it reduces the cost of my key bridge structures via distance maps.

I'm estimating the runtime budget: pruning to the top ~30 candidates and running full BFS-based evaluation on each keeps total time to a few hundred milliseconds, with bridge/triple minimum computations adding negligible overhead. I'm also weighing whether vectorizing the BFS with numpy across all sources simultaneously would actually beat the simple deque-based approach, since batching all 12 sources into one array could amortize the iteration cost.

Setting up the vectorized distance array...

Actually 40 iterations across 169 candidates is too slow at ~0.7s, so I should restrict to the top ~60 candidates by pre-score to get closer to 250ms, plus adaptive time checks. I'll also compute source distances once for pre-scoring versus the fuller candidate evaluation, and handle the opening move as a special case—just return a near-center empty cell rather than running full evaluation. Writing layout detection logic...

To make this robust across all layout types, I'm defining a 2D position function for each cell so neighbors sit at unit distance apart, letting me order them by angle rather than hardcoding direction sequences per layout.

Checking that the sentinel padding used in the distance BFS correctly stays at infinity when indexed through the neighbor array, then thinking about how many iterations the Bellman-style update will need to converge.

For counting new wins after placing a stone, I'm sketching a function that temporarily sets the board, builds union-find groups for that player, then only checks empty cells adjacent to the newly formed group as candidates for wins — since any winning cell not touching the new group would have already been a win before the move, which contradicts the invariant that no wins existed prior to placing. This lets me restrict the win-scan to just neighbors of the placed stone's group rather than all empty cells.

Cost-wise, building the union-find and scanning empties runs a few hundred microseconds per candidate move, so across the full move budget it stays around a few hundred milliseconds — I'll add time checks to abort tactical search stages if it runs long, falling back to the best move found so far. Writing policy function...

Checking for immediate winning moves first, then checking if the opponent has multiple winning threats that need blocking. If there's only one forced block I take it, otherwise I look for double-threat moves for myself before falling back to deeper heuristics.
